This article provides a brief overview of energy supply and consumption, using statistics summarized in tables, of the countries and regions that produce and consume the most energy.

As of 2022, energy consumption is still about 80% from fossil fuels.[[3]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-Enerdata-3) The [Gulf States](Arab_states_of_the_Persian_Gulf "Arab states of the Persian Gulf"), [United States](United_States "United States"), and <Russia> are major energy exporters, with notable customers being the [European Union](European_Union "European Union") and <China>, where domestically not enough energy is produced in order to satisfy energy demand. Energy consumption generally increases about 1-2% per year,[[4]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-4) except for [solar and wind energy](Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") which averaged 20% per year in the 2010s.[[5]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-5)[[6]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-6)

Energy that is produced, like from [fossil fuels](Fossil_fuels "Fossil fuels"), is processed in order to make it suitable for consumption by end users. The energy supply chain from initial production and final consumption involves many different activities, causing a loss of useful energy ultimately,[[7]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-7) see [exergy](Exergy "Exergy").

Energy consumption per capita in North America is very high, while in less developed countries it is low and usually more renewable.[[8]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-8)[[9]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-9) There is a clear connection between energy consumption per capita, and GDP per capita. [[10]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-10)

Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), there was a significant decline in energy usage worldwide in 2020, but total energy demand worldwide had recovered by 2021, and has hit a record high in 2022.[[11]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-11)

A serious problem concerning energy production and consumption is [greenhouse gas emissions](Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions"). Of about 50 billion tonnes worldwide annual total greenhouse gas emissions,[[12]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-12) 36 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide was emitted due to energy (almost all from fossil fuels) in 2021.[[13]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-13) The goal set in the [Paris Agreement](Paris_Agreement "Paris Agreement") to [limit climate change](Climate_change_mitigation "Climate change mitigation") will be difficult to achieve.[[14]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-14) Many scenarios have been envisioned to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, usually by the name of [net zero by 2050](Net_zero "Net zero").

One of the largest organizations in this field, the [International Energy Agency](International_Energy_Agency "International Energy Agency") (IEA), sells yearly comprehensive energy data which makes this data [paywalled](Paywall "Paywall") and [difficult to access for internet users](International_Energy_Agency#Restricting_access_to_data "International Energy Agency").[[15]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-balances-15) The organization Enerdata on the other hand publishes a free Yearbook, making the data more accessible.[[3]](World_energy_supply_and_consumption#cite_note-Enerdata-3) Another trustworthy organization that provides accurate energy data, mainly referring to the USA, is the [U.S. Energy Information Administration](U.S._Energy_Information_Administration "U.S. Energy Information Administration").

### Discussion about energy loss

There are different [qualities of energy](Energy_quality "Energy quality"). Heat, especially at a relatively low temperature, is low-quality energy, whereas electricity is high-quality energy. It takes around 3 kWh of heat to produce 1 kWh of electricity. But by the same token, a kilowatt-hour of this high-quality electricity can be used to pump several kilowatt-hours of heat into a building using a heat pump. And electricity can be used in many ways in which heat cannot. So the loss of energy incurred in thermal electricity plants is not comparable to a loss due to, say, resistance in power lines, because of quality difference.

In fact, the loss in thermal plants is due to poor conversion of chemical energy of fuel to electricity by combustion. Chemical energy of fuel is not low-quality because conversion to electricity in [fuel cells](Fuel_cell "Fuel cell") can be much more efficient than in thermal plants. So energy loss in thermal plants is real loss.

China is the [world's leader in electricity production from renewable energy sources](List_of_countries_by_electricity_production_from_renewable_sources "List of countries by electricity production from renewable sources"), with over triple the generation of the second-ranking country, the United States. China's [renewable energy](Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") sector is growing faster than its [fossil fuels](Fossil_fuels "Fossil fuels") and [nuclear power](Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") capacity, and is expected to contribute 43 per cent of global renewable capacity growth.[[1]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-scmp.com-1) China's total renewable energy capacity exceeded 1,000 GW in 2021, accounting for 43.5 per cent of the country's total power generation capacity, 10.2 percentage points higher than in 2015. The country aims to have 80 per cent of its total energy mix come from non-fossil fuel sources by 2060, and achieve a combined 1,200 GW of solar and wind capacity by 2030.[[1]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-scmp.com-1) In 2023, it was reported that China was on track to reach 1,371 gigawatts of wind and solar by 2025, five years ahead of target due to new renewables installations breaking records.[[2]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-2)

Although China currently has the world's largest installed capacity of hydro, solar and wind power, its energy needs are so large that in 2019, renewable sources provided 26% of its electricity generation[[3]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-3)—compared to 17% in the U.S.[[4]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-4)—with most of the remainder provided by coal power plants.
In early 2020, renewable energy comprised about 40% of China's total installed electric power capacity, and 26% of total power generation. By 2021, it had grown to 29.4% of total power generation. The share of renewables in total power generation is expected to continue increasing to 36% by 2025,[[5]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-5) in line with China's pledge to achieve [carbon neutrality](Carbon_neutrality "Carbon neutrality") before 2060 and peak emissions before 2030.

China sees renewables as a source of [energy security](Energy_security "Energy security") and not just only to reduce [carbon emission](Carbon_emission "Carbon emission").[[6]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-6) China's Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Air Pollution issued by China's State Council in September 2013, illustrates the government's desire to increase the share of renewables in China's [energy mix](Energy_mix "Energy mix").[[7]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-:0-7) Unlike oil, coal and gas, the supplies of which are finite and subject to geopolitical tensions, renewable energy systems can be built and used wherever there is sufficient water, wind, and sun.[[8]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-chinaen-8)

China is also major leader of clean energy technology.[[9]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-:322-9): 98 As Chinese renewable manufacturing has grown, the costs of renewable energy technologies have dropped dramatically due to both innovation and economies of scale from market expansion.[[8]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-chinaen-8) In 2015, China became the world's largest producer of [photovoltaic power](Photovoltaic_power "Photovoltaic power"), with 43 GW of total installed capacity.[[10]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-10)[[11]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-11) From 2005 to 2014, production of [solar cells](Solar_cells "Solar cells") in China has expanded 100-fold.[[8]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-chinaen-8) However, China is not expected to achieve grid parity – when an alternate source of energy is as cheap or cheaper than power purchased from the grid—until 2022.[[12]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-12)

The country is the world's largest investor in renewable energy, with the country's companies accounting for four of the world's five biggest renewable energy deals made in 2016.[[13]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-13) In 2017, investments in renewable energy amounted to US$279.8 billion worldwide, with China accounting for US$126.6 billion or 45% of the global investments.[[14]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-14) According to researcher Dr Cornelia Tremann, "China has since become the world's largest investor, producer and consumer of renewable energy worldwide, manufacturing state-of-the-art solar panels, wind turbines and hydroelectric energy facilities" as well as becoming the world's largest producer of electric cars and buses.[[15]](Renewable_energy_in_China#cite_note-15)

According to data from the [US Energy Information Administration](Energy_Information_Administration "Energy Information Administration"), [renewable energy](Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") accounted for about 13.1% of total primary energy consumption and about 21.5% of total utility-scale electricity generation in the United States in 2022.[[2]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-EIAmonthlyElectricity-2)[[3]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-3)

Since 2019, [wind power](Wind_power "Wind power") has been the largest producer of renewable electricity in the country. Wind power generated 434.8 [terawatt-hours](Terawatt-hour "Terawatt-hour") of electricity in 2022, which accounted for 10.25% of the nation's total electricity generation and 47.6% of the total renewable electricity generation.[[2]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-EIAmonthlyElectricity-2) By January 2023, the United States [nameplate generating capacity](Nameplate_capacity "Nameplate capacity") for [wind power](Wind_power_in_the_United_States "Wind power in the United States") was 141,300 megawatts (MW).[[4]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-acpaQ3_2021-4) [Texas](Wind_power_in_Texas "Wind power in Texas") remained firmly established as the leader in wind power deployment, followed by Iowa and Oklahoma as of the first quarter of 2023.[[5]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-DOEWindExchange-5)

[Hydroelectric power](Hydroelectric_power "Hydroelectric power") is the second-largest producer of renewable electricity in the country, generating around 6.5% of the nation's total electricity in 2022 as well as 28.7% of the total renewable electricity generation.[[2]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-EIAmonthlyElectricity-2) The United States is the [fourth largest producer](Hydroelectricity#World_hydroelectric_capacity "Hydroelectricity") of hydroelectricity in the world after China, Canada and Brazil.

Solar power provides a growing share of electricity in the country, with over 155 GW of installed capacity generating about 3.43% of the country's total electricity supply in 2022, up from 2.8% the previous year.
As of 202, more than 260,000 people worked in the solar industry and [43 states deployed net metering](Net_metering_in_the_United_States "Net metering in the United States"), where energy utilities bought back excess power generated by [solar arrays](Solar_array "Solar array").[[6]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-6)[[7]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-7) Large [photovoltaic power plants](Photovoltaic_power_plant "Photovoltaic power plant") in the United States include [Mount Signal Solar](Mount_Signal_Solar "Mount Signal Solar") (600 MW) and [Solar Star](Solar_Star "Solar Star") (579 MW). Since the United States pioneered [solar thermal power](Solar_thermal_power "Solar thermal power") technology in the 1980s with [Solar One](The_Solar_Project "The Solar Project"), several more such power stations have been built. The largest of these solar thermal power stations are the [Ivanpah Solar Power Facility](Ivanpah_Solar_Power_Facility "Ivanpah Solar Power Facility") (392 MW), southwest of Las Vegas, and the <SEGS> group of plants in the Mojave Desert, with a total generating capacity of 354 MW.[[8]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-segs-8)

Other renewable energy sources include [geothermal](Geothermal_energy "Geothermal energy"), with [The Geysers](The_Geysers "The Geysers") in [Northern California](Northern_California "Northern California") the largest geothermal complex in the world.

The development of renewable energy and energy efficiency marked "a new era of energy exploration" in the United States, according to former President [Barack Obama](Barack_Obama "Barack Obama").[[9]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-9) In a [joint address to the Congress](Joint_address_to_the_Congress "Joint address to the Congress") on February 24, 2009, President Obama called for doubling renewable energy within the following three years. Renewable energy reached a major milestone in the first quarter of 2011, when it contributed 11.7% of total national energy production (660 TWh), surpassing energy production from nuclear power (620 TWh)[[10]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-10) for the first time since 1997.[[11]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-11) In his 2012 [State of the Union](State_of_the_Union "State of the Union") address, President Barack Obama restated his commitment to renewable energy and mentioned the long-standing Interior Department commitment to permit 10,000 MW of renewable energy projects on public land in 2012.[[12]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Lindsay_Morris-12) Under President [Joe Biden](Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"), Congress increased that goal to 25,000 MW (25 GW) by 2025.[[13]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-13) As of May 2023, the Bureau of Land Management has approved projects meeting approximately 37% of that goal.[[14]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-14)

## Rationale for renewables

Renewable energy technologies encompass a broad, diverse array of technologies, including [solar photovoltaics](Photovoltaics "Photovoltaics"), [solar thermal power](Solar_thermal_power "Solar thermal power") plants and heating/cooling systems, [wind farms](Wind_farm "Wind farm"), [hydroelectricity](Hydroelectricity "Hydroelectricity"), [geothermal power](Geothermal_power "Geothermal power") plants, and [ocean power systems](Wave_power "Wave power") and the use of [biomass](Biomass "Biomass").

The report *[Outlook On Renewable Energy In America](Outlook_On_Renewable_Energy_In_America "Outlook On Renewable Energy In America")* explains that America needs renewable energy, for many reasons:
> America needs energy that is secure, reliable, improves public health, protects the environment, addresses climate change, creates jobs, and provides technological leadership. America needs renewable energy. If renewable energy is to be developed to its full potential, America will need coordinated, sustained federal and state policies that expand renewable energy markets; promote and deploy new technology; and provide appropriate opportunities to encourage renewable energy use in all critical energy market sectors: wholesale and distributed electricity generation, thermal energy applications, and transportation.[[15]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-15)

Another benefit of some renewable energy technologies, like wind and solar photovoltaics (PV) is that they require little or no water to generate electricity whereas thermoelectric (fossil fuel-based) power plants require vast amounts of water for operation.

In 2009, President [Barack Obama](Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in the [inaugural address](United_States_presidential_inauguration "United States presidential inauguration") called for the expanded use of renewable energy to meet the twin challenges of [energy security](Energy_security "Energy security") and [climate change](Climate_change "Climate change"). Those were the first references ever to the nation's energy use, to renewable resources, and to climate change in an inauguration speech of a United States president. President Obama looked to the near future, saying that as a nation, the United States will "harness the sun and the winds and the soil to fuel our cars and run our factories."[[16]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-apps1.eere.energy.gov-16)

The president's *[New Energy For America](New_Energy_For_America "New Energy For America")* plan calls for a federal investment of $150 billion over the next decade to catalyze private efforts to build a clean energy future. Specifically, the plan calls for renewable energy to supply 10% of the nation's electricity by 2012, rising to 25% by 2025.[[16]](Renewable_energy_in_the_United_States#cite_note-apps1.eere.energy.gov

As of 2018, renewable energy accounted for 79% of the domestically produced [electricity used in Brazil](Electricity_sector_in_Brazil "Electricity sector in Brazil").[[1]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-:0-1)[[2]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-:1-2)[[3]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-3)

Brazil relies on [hydroelectricity](Hydroelectricity "Hydroelectricity") for 65% of its electricity,[[1]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-:0-1)[[2]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-:1-2) and the Brazilian government plans to expand the share of [wind energy](Wind_energy "Wind energy") (currently 11%), [solar energy](Solar_energy "Solar energy") (currently 2.5%) and [biomass](Biomass "Biomass")[[1]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-:0-1)[[2]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-:1-2) as alternatives. Wind energy has the greatest potential in Brazil during the [dry season](Dry_season "Dry season"), so it is considered a [hedge](Hedge_(finance) "Hedge (finance)") against low [rainfall](Rainfall "Rainfall") and the geographical spread of existing hydroelectric resources.

Brazil held its first wind-only energy auction in 2009, in a move to diversify its [energy portfolio](Energy_in_Brazil "Energy in Brazil"). Foreign companies scrambled to take part.
The bidding lead to the construction of 2 [gigawatts](Gigawatts "Gigawatts") (GW) of wind production with an investment of about $6 billion over the following two years.
Brazil's technical potential for wind energy is 143 GW due to the country's blustery 7,400 kilometres (4,600 mi) kilometres [coastline](Coastline_of_Brazil "Coastline of Brazil") where most projects are based.
The Brazilian Wind Energy Association and the government have set a goal of achieving 20 GW of wind energy capacity by 2020 from the current 5 GW (2014).[[4]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-4) The industry hopes the auction will help kick-start the wind-energy sector, which already accounts for 70% of the total in all of Latin America.[[5]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-5)

According to Brazil's Energy Master-plan 2016-2026 (PDE2016-2026), Brazil is expected to install 18,5GW of additional wind power generation, 84% in the North-East and 14% in the South.[[1]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-:0-1)

Brazil started focusing on developing alternative sources of energy, mainly [sugarcane ethanol](Ethanol_fuel_in_Brazil "Ethanol fuel in Brazil"), after the oil shocks in the 1970s.
Brazil's large [sugarcane](Sugarcane "Sugarcane") farms helped the development.
In 1985, 91% of cars produced that year ran on sugarcane ethanol.
The success of [flexible-fuel vehicles](Flexible-fuel_vehicle "Flexible-fuel vehicle"), introduced in 2003, together with the mandatory E25 blend throughout the country, have allowed ethanol fuel consumption in the country to achieve a 50% market share of the gasoline-powered fleet by February 2008.[[6]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-ANP07_2008-6)[[7]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-7)

## Total energy matrix and Electric energy matrix

The main characteristic of the Brazilian energy matrix is that it is much more renewable than that of the world. While in 2019 the world matrix was only 14% made up of renewable energy, Brazil's was at 45%. Petroleum and oil products made up 34.3% of the matrix; sugar cane derivatives, 18%; hydraulic energy, 12.4%; natural gas, 12.2%; firewood and charcoal, 8.8%; varied renewable energies, 7%; mineral coal, 5.3%; nuclear, 1.4%, and other non-renewable energies, 0.6%.[[8]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-Matriz_Energética_e_Elétrica-8)

In the electric energy matrix, the difference between Brazil and the world is even greater: while the world only had 25% of renewable electric energy in 2019, Brazil had 83%. The Brazilian electric matrix is composed of: hydraulic energy, 64.9%; biomass, 8.4%; wind energy, 8.6%; solar energy, 1%; natural gas, 9.3%; oil products, 2%; nuclear, 2.5%; coal and derivatives, 3.3%.[[8]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-Matriz_Energética_e_Elétrica-8)

## Electricity

### Hydroelectricity

[Hydroelectric power plants](Hydroelectric_power_plant "Hydroelectric power plant") produced almost 80% of the electrical energy consumed in Brazil (now 60%).[[9]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-9) Brazil has the third highest potential for hydroelectricity, following Russia and China.[[10]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-10) At the end of 2021 Brazil was the 2nd country in the world in terms of installed [hydroelectric power](Hydroelectric_power "Hydroelectric power") (109.4 GW).[[11]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-11)

#### Itaipu power plant

Main article: [Itaipu Dam](Itaipu_Dam "Itaipu Dam")

The [Itaipu Dam](Itaipu_Dam "Itaipu Dam") is the world's second largest hydroelectric power station by installed capacity.
Built on the [Paraná River](Paran%C3%A1_River "Paraná River") dividing Brazil and <Paraguay>, the dam provides over 75% of Paraguay's electric power needs, and meets more than 20% of Brazil's total electricity demand.
The river runs along the border of the two countries, and during the initial diplomatic talks for the dam construction both countries were suffering from droughts.
The original goal was therefore to provide better management and utilization of water resources for the irrigation of crops.
Argentina was also later incorporated in some of the governmental planning and agreements because it is directly affected, being downstream, by the regulation of the water on the river.
If the dam were to completely open the water flow, areas as far south as [Buenos Aires](Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires") could potentially flood.

Construction of the dam started in 1975, and the first generator was opened in 1983.
It is estimated that 10,000 locals were displaced by the construction of the dam, and around 40,000 people were hired to help with the construction of the project.
Many environmental concerns were overlooked when constructing the dam, due to the trade-off considering the production of such a large amount of energy without carbon emissions, and no immediate harmful byproducts, such as with [nuclear energy](Nuclear_power "Nuclear power").

### Wind power

In July 2022 Brazil reached 22 GW of installed wind power.[[12]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-12)[[13]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-13) In 2021 Brazil was the 7th country in the world in terms of installed wind power (21 GW),[[14]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-RENEWABLE_CAPACITY_STATISTICS_2021-14)[[15]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-15) and the 4th largest producer of wind energy in the world (72 TWh), behind only China, USA and Germany.[[16]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-auto-16)

As of August 2021, the total installed wind power capacity in Brazil was 18.9 GW, with 16.4 GW in the [Northeast Region](Northeast_Region%2C_Brazil "Northeast Region, Brazil") and 2.0 GW in the [South Region](South_Region%2C_Brazil "South Region, Brazil").[[17]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-17)

Wind is more intense from June to December, coinciding with the months of lower rainfall intensity.
This puts the wind as a potential complementary source of energy to hydroelectricity.[[18]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-18)

Brazil's first wind energy turbine was installed in [Fernando de Noronha](Fernando_de_Noronha "Fernando de Noronha") Archipelago in 1992.
Ten years later the government created the Program for Incentive of Alternative Electric Energy Sources (Proinfa) to encourage the use of other renewable sources, such as wind power, biomass, and small hydro.
Since the inception of Proinfa, Brazil's wind energy production has grown from 22 MW in 2003 to 602 MW in 2009, and to over 8,700 MW by 2015.

Developing these wind power sources in Brazil is helping the country to meet its strategic objectives of enhancing [energy security](Energy_security "Energy security"), reducing greenhouse gas emissions and creating jobs.
The potential for this type of power generation in Brazil could reach up to 145,000 MW, according to the 2001 Brazilian Wind Power Potential Report by the Electric Energy Research Centre (Cepel).

While the [2009 United Nations Climate Change Conference](2009_United_Nations_Climate_Change_Conference "2009 United Nations Climate Change Conference") (COP15) was taking place in <Copenhagen>, Brazil's National Electric Energy Agency (<ANEEL>) held the country's first ever wind-only energy auction.
On December 14, 2009, around 1,800 megawatts (MW) were contracted with energy from 71 wind power plants scheduled to be delivered beginning July 1, 2012. The 716 MW Lagoa dos Ventos began operating in 2021.[[19]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-19)

### Solar power

Main article: [Solar power in Brazil](Solar_power_in_Brazil "Solar power in Brazil")

In October 2022 Brazil reached 22 GW of installed solar power.[[20]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-20)[[21]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-21) In 2021, Brazil was the 14th country in the world in terms of installed solar power (13 GW),[[22]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-22) and the 11th largest producer of solar energy in the world (16.8 TWh).[[16]](Renewable_energy_in_Brazil#cite_note-auto-16)

India is world's 3rd largest consumer of electricity and world's 3rd largest [renewable energy](Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") producer with 40% of energy capacity installed in the year 2022 (160 GW of 400 GW) coming from renewable sources.[[1]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-reca1-1)[[2]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-2) [Ernst & Young](Ernst_%26_Young "Ernst & Young")'s (EY) 2021 Renewable Energy Country Attractiveness Index (RECAI) ranked India 3rd behind USA and China.[[3]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-rec2-3)[[4]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-rec3-4) In FY2023-24, India is planning to issue 50 GW tenders for wind, solar and hybrid projects.[[5]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-5) India has committed for a goal of 500 GW renewable energy capacity by 2030.[[6]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-6)In line with this commitment, India's installed renewable energy capacity has been experiencing a steady upward trend. From 94.4 GW in 2021, the capacity has gone up to 119.1 GW in 2023 as of Q4.[[7]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-7)

In 2016, [Paris Agreement](Paris_Agreement "Paris Agreement")'s [Intended Nationally Determined Contributions](Intended_Nationally_Determined_Contributions "Intended Nationally Determined Contributions") targets, India made commitment of producing 50% of its total electricity from [non-fossil fuel](Fossil_fuel "Fossil fuel") sources by 2030.[[8]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-8)[[9]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-:1-9) In 2018, India's [Central Electricity Authority](Central_Electricity_Authority_(India) "Central Electricity Authority (India)") set a target of producing 50% of the total electricity from non-[fossil fuels](Fossil_fuels "Fossil fuels") sources by 2030.[[10]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-:6-10) India has also set a target of producing 175 GW by 2022 and 500 GW by 2030 from renewable energy.[[11]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-new1-11)[[10]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-:6-10)[[12]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-mnreRenewableBreakup-12)[[13]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-scheme-wise-progress-13)

Solar, wind and [run-of-the-river hydroelectricity](Run-of-the-river_hydroelectricity "Run-of-the-river hydroelectricity") are environment-friendly cheaper power sources they are used as ""must-run" sources in India to cater for the [base load](Base_load "Base load"), and the polluting and foreign-import dependent [coal-fired power](Coal-fired_power_station "Coal-fired power station") is increasingly being moved from the "must-run base load" power generation to the [load following power generation](Load_following_power_plant "Load following power plant") (mid-priced and mid-merit on-demand need-based intermittently-produced electricity) to meet the [peaking demand](Peak_demand "Peak demand") only.[[16]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-16) Some of the daily peak demand in India is already met with the renewable peaking hydro power capacity. Solar and wind power with 4-hour battery storage systems, as a source of dispatchable generation compared with new coal and new gas plants, is already cost-competitive in India without subsidy.[[17]](Renewable_energy_in_India#cite_note-17)

India initiated the [International Solar Alliance](International_Solar_Alliance "International Solar Alliance") (ISA), an alliance of 121 countries. India was world's first country to set up a ministry of [non-conventional energy](Non-conventional_energy "Non-conventional energy") resources ([Ministry of New and Renewable Energy](Ministry_of_New_and_Renewable_Energy "Ministry of New and Renewable Energy") (MNRE) in early 1980s) . [Solar Energy Corporation of India](Solar_Energy_Corporation_of_India "Solar Energy Corporation of India") (SECI), a [public sector undertaking](Public_sector_undertakings_in_India "Public sector undertakings in India"), is responsible for the development of solar energy industry in India.
